title: Agents and scopes
text: Using MemCommit Agents and scopes Several agents can read each other's memories as premises. Scopes decide who may read and write, and a blackboard coordinates the work. On this page Scopes The blackboard Traces and handoffs Scopes A memory's scope says who may read it. shared is for every agent; a scope named after an agent ( planner ) or under it ( planner/drafts ) is that agent's own. An AgentSession reads shared plus the agent's own scopes and stamps every write with the agent's name. from memcommit import AgentSession, scope_guard store.guard(scope_guard) # an agent may put only into shared or its own scopes planner = AgentSession(store, "planner", reads=["research"]) planner.put("plan", "trip", {"steps": ["book"]}, scope="planner/drafts") planner.find(kind="plan") scope_guard is enforced at commit for every agent. The system agent may write anywhere. The blackboard from memcommit import Blackboard class Writer: name = "writer" consumes = frozenset({"finding"}) def handle(self, finding, tx, session): tx.put("brief", finding.key, {"text": "..."}, derived_from=[finding.id]) board = Blackboard(store, [Researcher(), Writer()]) board.run() Agents consume kinds of memory and write results. An agent's results and a receipt commit together, so work is done exactly once, survives a restart, and is redone when its inputs go stale. An agent that names what it produces runs upstream of its consumers. A failing agent writes nothing but an error memory in its own scope. Traces and handoffs memcommit.trace(store, agent, task) records a run as a root and a tree of typed steps ( thought , action , observation , message , result , error ). t.handoff(agent, task) starts another agent's sub-trace derived from a message step. See Sessions for the conversational form. Previous Working memory Next Audit and defense

title: Audit and defense
text: Using MemCommit Audit and defense Shared memory is an attack surface. MemCommit does not decide what is malicious, but it makes a defender's work exact. On this page Tools A typical repair Why it works Tools Tool What it does verify(store) Replays the log and returns problems: altered bodies, records out of order, provenance to memories that did not exist, writes into another agent's scope. An empty list is ok. lineage(store, id) Everything a memory was built on. blast_radius(store, refs) Everything built on a reference, in any status. quarantine(store, ids, reason) Retracts suspects and marks what was built on them stale, in one transaction. diff(store, a, b) Memories whose status or tier changed between two LSNs. provenance_guard() Rejects at write time a memory built on a memory that is missing or no longer holds. seal(store) Writes a hash chain over the log; verify rechecks it, so a deleted or reordered record is caught. scope_guard An agent writes only to shared or its own scopes. A typical repair from memcommit import blast_radius, quarantine, verify affected = blast_radius(store, [bad_observation.id]) # what the bad observation reached quarantine(store, [bad_observation.id], "tool was compromised") assert verify(store) == [] The agents on a blackboard then redo only the work that went stale. Because notes and replies record what they were derived from, the same repair reaches notes learned from a spoofed session. Why it works Memories are content-addressed, so an altered body no longer hashes to its id. The log is append-only, so verify can replay it for what a well-behaved store could not have written. Provenance is a graph, so the reach of a bad memory is a query. See Provenance . Previous Agents and scopes Next Command line

title: Benchmarks
text: Reference Benchmarks Both benchmarks are synthetic, so they show behaviour, not real-world accuracy. Both are deterministic and need no model. On this page Does memory help? Which eviction policy? Does memory help? python examples/memory_benchmark.py writes results/memory/ . 20 users chat with an assistant over 8, 32, or 64 sessions each. Facts come up in passing, one is a request to remember, 40% of users move cities later, and the rest is chatter with distractors. Half the statements are in forms the built-in extractor is built for and half are paraphrases it cannot parse. Each user is then asked their current city, dog, drink, and locker code. A recency-aware reader answers from whatever each configuration retrieves: right if the latest-mentioned value the user ever gave is the current one. Means over 3 seeds. Configuration 8 sessions 32 sessions 64 sessions Context words at 64 none 0.000 0.000 0.000 0 full history in context 1.000 1.000 1.000 1,358 episodic search only 0.958 0.958 0.958 20 notes from dreaming only 0.492 0.512 0.487 15 episodic + notes 0.942 0.971 0.958 35 notes from dreaming, oracle extractor 1.000 1.000 1.000 12 episodic + notes, oracle extractor 1.000 1.000 1.000 33 What it shows: Search over the record reads about 20 words where the full history needs up to 1,358, and is right 96% of the time. Its misses are facts that changed. With a perfect extractor the notes are right every time from 12 words, because the later statement supersedes the old note. With the built-in rule extractor, which parses half the phrasings, they are right about half the time, and the two tiers together only match search alone. The extractor is the limit, not the pipeline. Saving by tool call alone catches only explicit requests, so it scores about 0.11 to 0.15. Warning The paraphrases were written to share a stem with the questions, which favours lexical search, and the first version of this benchmark gave the extractor text written to match it and scored 1.000, which was circular. Both are stated in results/memory/README.md . Which eviction policy? python examples/policy_benchmark.py writes results/policies/ . A synthetic agent-shaped workload (60 tasks writing 6 trace steps each, then 472 skewed reuses) is replayed through the real store under each policy, and the hit rate of working memory is measured at capacities 16, 32, and 64, with the cost in log records and replay time. Policy Hit rate, cap 16 cap 32 cap 64 FIFO 0.506 0.551 0.602 LRU 0.642 0.744 0.828 LFU 0.354 0.460 0.606 Forgetting curve 0.648 0.771 0.867 ARC 0.551 0.663 0.763 Learned (online logistic) 0.627 0.742 0.803 The forgetting curve does best under the cap and also writes the fewest log records, since every miss is a page-in and an eviction. LFU and 2Q do poorly because this workload reuses fresh trace steps often, and both evict memories used only once first. Which policy wins depends on the workload, which is why policies are pluggable and the benchmark can replay a recorded one ( AccessLog(record=True) , then bench.from_access_log ). Previous API at a glance Next Leaderboard

title: Command line
text: Reference Command line Every command takes a store path; the suffix picks the engine (.db for SQLite, .jsonl for JSON lines). On this page Commands Example Commands Command What it does memcommit demo [--path demo.db] Run the end-to-end sample agent. With --path , keep its store. memcommit index memory.db [--agent assistant] [--max-chars 4000] Print the catalog of notes. memcommit search memory.db "query" [--where W] [-k 5] [--agent assistant] Search notes, episodes, or both; prints JSON. W is derived (default), episodic , or all . memcommit dream memory.db [--dry-run] Run an offline consolidation pass; lists each change. memcommit verify memory.db Replay the log and report problems. Prints ok ; exits 1 on problems. memcommit stats memory.db Counts by status, tier, and kind. memcommit compact memory.db [--retain-archive-seconds N] Fold the log, purging old archived memories if asked. memcommit serve memory.db [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 7340] [--snapshot state.json] Serve a store to agents in other processes. python -m memcommit is the same command. Example memcommit demo --path demo.db memcommit stats demo.db memcommit index demo.db memcommit search demo.db "dog" --where all memcommit dream demo.db --dry-run memcommit verify demo.db Previous Audit and defense Next API at a glance

title: Concepts
text: Getting started Concepts A memory is an immutable value. Everything that changes about it is a record in a log, and state is what replaying the log gives. On this page Memories The log Status Tier Provenance Two kinds of memory Memories A Memory is a JSON value with a kind (what sort of thing it is), a key (what it is about), a body , a source (the agent that wrote it), a scope (who may read it), an importance , and derived_from (what it was built on). Its id is a hash of all of that, so writing the same memory twice names the same memory, and work redone with the same result restores what was there. The log Every change is a record: put , restore , stale , retract , or move . Records are numbered (LSN) and grouped into transactions, which are all or nothing. The store's state is a fold over the log, so as_of(lsn) rebuilds any past state, and rollback writes compensating records instead of erasing anything. Status Status says whether a memory holds. Status Meaning live It holds. stale Something it was built on no longer holds. Redone work may bring it back. retracted It was wrong. Tier Tier says where a memory sits, which is what retrieval and policies act on. Tier Holds short Working memory, bounded: new memories, an agent's context. A cache. mid Optional: evicted memories grouped into segments (by trace). long Consolidated memories and summaries. archive Everything evicted or compacted. Searched on request; paged back in on use. Status and tier are independent: a stale long-term memory is still long-term. Provenance derived_from names the memories (and outside references like doc:handbook@3 ) a memory was built on. When one of them goes stale or is retracted, everything built on it goes stale, transitively, in one transaction. A memory can also derive from a read ( query_ref ), so work that saw "nothing known" is redone when something becomes known. See Provenance . Two kinds of memory Episodic memory is the record: sessions, turns, and tool calls, as they happened. Derived memory is what was learned: notes at paths. A note names the episodes it came from, so the detail is one fetch away, and a bad episode takes its notes with it. Previous Install and run the demo Next Playground

title: Decisions
text: Project Decisions A log of choices, newest last: what was chosen, what else was possible, why, and what it costs. On this page 2026-10-21: Rename Mneme to MemCommit 2026-10-21: MIT license for the code 2026-10-21: A generic core, a declared structure on top 2026-10-21: The schema is a guard, and itself a memory 2026-10-21: A small JSON-schema subset, no dependency 2026-10-21: A kind can require its premises 2026-10-21: A session is a trace, not a new structure 2026-10-21: A reply derives from what it read 2026-10-21: Derived memory is notes at paths, with a generated index 2026-10-21: Updates supersede; deletes retract 2026-10-21: Five tools over two tiers 2026-10-21: Dreaming is an offline pass with a pluggable extractor 2026-10-21: The log decides where a pass starts 2026-10-21: Conflicts resolve by supersession, not by judgement 2026-10-21: Maintenance archives, it does not delete 2026-10-21: A pass can be previewed and undone 2026-10-21: Measure retrieval with a recency-aware reader, not a model 2026-10-21: Report the result that is unflattering 2026-10-21: Stem and drop stopwords in the lexical index 2026-10-21: Fix a circular benchmark rather than report it 2026-10-21: A demo that needs no model 2026-10-21: Manuals share one design, and each has a demo that replays real output 2026-10-21: Serve the manuals from lamng3.com 2026-10-22: Playgrounds run in the browser, and say what they are 2026-10-23: A line-by-line visualizer, served under the manual 2026-10-21: Rename Mneme to MemCommit Choice. The project is MemCommit: repo lamng3/memcommit , package and CLI memcommit . Alternatives. Keep Mneme; MemJournal, MemTx, MemCatalog, MemLake, MemLineage. Why. "Mem" plus a database word people already know. "Commit" names the one guarantee every write has: it is atomic, logged, and attributable. Three syllables, free on PyPI. Cost. Every importer changed: kroma , aegis , agentic-ontologist , and the ontodb README. The OntoDB engine's RDF namespace moved from urn:mneme: to urn:memcommit: , so a database written before the rename needs its namespace migrated. The library was pre-alpha and none were kept. 2026-10-21: MIT license for the code Choice. MIT. The paper keeps its own text license. Alternatives. CC BY 4.0 (what the repo had), Apache-2.0. Why. Creative Commons advises against its licenses for software: CC BY says nothing about patents or about source distribution. MIT is the shortest license people recognize, and the library has no dependencies to reconcile with. Cost. None the project cares about; Apache-2.0's patent grant is the one thing given up. 2026-10-21: A generic core, a declared structure on top Choice. The core names no domain. A project declares its own memory structure with Schema and Kind , and the store enforces it with a guard. Alternatives. Hard-code the kinds the Agentic Ontologist uses; leave bodies free-form and document conventions. Why. The Agentic Ontologist's structure lived as constants ( QUESTION , ANSWER ) in its own integration, enforced by nothing. A declared structure makes the same idea reusable and checkable, and lets an agent read what it may write. Cost. One more concept to learn. It is optional: a store with no schema behaves as before. 2026-10-21: The schema is a guard, and itself a memory Choice. Schema.attach(store) adds a commit guard and writes the schema to the log as a schema memory. A changed schema writes a new one and marks the old one stale. Alternatives. Validate in a wrapper around put only; keep the schema outside the log; stamp each memory with a schema version in derived_from . Why. A guard holds for every writer in every process, including the server and the blackboard, and it sees a whole commit, so requires can be satisfied by a premise written in the same transaction. Putting the schema in the log means as_of(lsn) also shows which structure held then. Stamping each memory with a version in derived_from would stale all data on every schema change, which is the wrong blas

title: Dreaming
text: Using MemCommit Dreaming An agent that saves notes by tool call only remembers what it thought to save. A dreaming pass finds what was implied, and maintains the store. On this page Run a pass What a pass does Extractors When to run What a pass records Repair and undo Run a pass from memcommit import Dreamer dreamer = Dreamer(store) # or Dreamer(store, extractor=my_model_extractor) dreamer.run(dry_run=True).changes # what it would do, without writing report = dreamer.run() # do it dreamer.undo(report) # take it back, if nobody else has written since A pass reads the sessions that ended since the last pass, asks an extractor for the learnings in each, and writes them as notes derived from the session and the turns they came from. Then it maintains the store. What a pass does Step Effect Extract Each learning becomes a note at its path, derived from the session and its source turns. Conflicts A learning whose path holds a different note replaces it. The old version goes stale, with what was built on it. The last statement in a session wins. Duplicates Live notes in the same directory with word overlap of at least 0.85 are merged: the most important is kept, the rest go to the archive. Oversized A note over max_chars (1200) is split at paragraph breaks into -part-N notes derived from it, and the original goes to the archive. Extractors An Extractor is a function from a Session to a list of Learning(path, text, title, tags, importance, sources) . The built-in heuristic_extractor needs no model. It finds statements the user made about where they live, "my X is Y", "I prefer Y", and "remember that Y", and it records a sequence of two or more tool calls that ended well as a playbook. The memory tools' own calls are not counted. A language model is a function with the same signature. Warning The built-in extractor parses only the phrasings it has patterns for. On the synthetic benchmark it finds about half of the facts, and an oracle extractor finds all of them. See Benchmarks . Pass a model-backed extractor for real use. When to run dreamer.due(min_sessions=3) # have enough sessions ended? dreamer.attach(min_sessions=3) # run a pass whenever enough sessions have ended memcommit dream memory.db runs one from the command line, and --dry-run previews it. What a pass records A pass writes a dream memory recording the log position it covered, derived from the sessions it read. The next pass starts from the highest position recorded, counting records of any status, so a pass whose source session was later retracted is not run again. dreamer.watermark() returns it. Repair and undo Every edit is a transaction with provenance. Retract a bad session and the notes learned from it go stale. undo(report) rolls the log back to before the pass using compensating records, so history is kept, and refuses if any other agent has written since. An undone pass is not retried automatically. Previous Notes Next Search and recall

title: A transactional memory layer for agents
text: A transactional memory layer for agents MemCommit keeps what agents did and learned as memories in one append-only log, with provenance, tiers, a declared structure, and an offline pass that turns finished sessions into notes. $ git clone https://github.com/lamng3/memcommit.git && cd memcommit $ pip install -e . && memcommit demo Get started Concepts Playground Showcase Time-travel a real memory log replay of a real run Try it: Click a memory, then Retract selected, and watch what was built on it go stale. Drag the slider to go back in time. lsn 0 Retract selected Roll back Reset Pick a memory, then retract it: everything derived from it goes stale, in one transaction. Drag the slider to see the state at any log position. The log and the cascade come from the library; this page only replays them. What it does One append-only log holds what agents did and what they learned. Everything else is a fold over it. Showcase: visual walkthrough Step through the real code line by line: a write, a stale cascade, rollback, compaction, and where memory lives. Playground Write memories into a log in the browser, retract a premise, and watch the cascade. Declare a structure Kinds, scopes, and what must derive from what; every write is checked. Record sessions Each turn, tool call, and result is its own memory, committed as it happens. Keep notes Notes at paths, a generated index, five tools a model can call. Consolidate offline Extract, supersede, merge, split, and undo a whole pass. Invalidate by provenance Retract a premise and everything built on it goes stale. Check the claims A benchmark that says where the library helps and where it does not. An agent that remembers needs two things. It needs the full record of what happened, so detail is never lost. It also needs short notes of what matters, so it can read what it knows in a few lines. MemCommit keeps both, in one log, and records where every note came from. This manual describes how to install MemCommit, declare the structure of your memory, record sessions, keep and search notes, consolidate them offline, bound working memory, audit it, and run it from the command line. The last parts describe how it works inside and how the project is developed. What MemCommit does today Stores memories as immutable, content-addressed JSON values in an append-only log. Status ( live , stale , retracted ) and tier ( short , mid , long , archive ) come from replaying the log. See Concepts . Checks every write against a memory structure you declare. See Declare a memory structure . Records sessions as they happen: each turn, tool call, and result. See Sessions . Keeps notes at paths, with a generated index and five tools a model can call. See Notes . Consolidates sessions into notes offline, supersedes conflicting notes, merges duplicates, splits oversized ones, and can undo a pass. See Dreaming . Marks stale everything built on a premise that stops holding, in one transaction. See Provenance . Bounds working memory with a cache and replacement policies, and compacts both memories and the log. See Working memory and The database underneath . Note MemCommit is research software. Results so far are on synthetic workloads; see Benchmarks . Quick start git clone https://github.com/lamng3/memcommit.git cd memcommit pip install -e ".[dev]" memcommit demo The demo runs a scripted assistant, with no model and no network, through every part of the loop. See Install and run the demo .

title: Install and run the demo
text: Getting started Install and run the demo Python 3.11 or newer, no runtime dependencies. The demo shows the whole loop in a few seconds. On this page Install Run the demo Use it from Python Tests Install git clone https://github.com/lamng3/memcommit.git cd memcommit pip install -e ".[dev]" [dev] adds pytest and ruff. The library itself has no dependencies. Run the demo memcommit demo A scripted assistant talks to users over several sessions. The demo walks through eight steps: The structure is declared once, and every write is checked against it. Two users talk to the assistant; it keeps the full record of each session. Dreaming: an offline pass extracts what was implied, with provenance back to the turns. The next session starts with the index, then answers from notes. A fact changes; the pass supersedes the note, and what was built on the old one goes stale. An episode turns out to be spoofed; the notes learned from it go stale. A synthetic benchmark answers whether memory helps. The record verifies. memcommit demo --path demo.db keeps the store, so you can inspect it afterwards with the command line . Use it from Python import memcommit from memcommit import Dreamer, Knowledge, Session store = memcommit.open("memory.db") # SQLite; .jsonl works too; MemoryStore() is in memory with Session.start(store, "assistant", user="alice") as session: session.user_says("I live in Lyon, and my dog is named Rex.") session.agent_says("Noted.") Dreamer(store).run() # turns the session into notes notes = Knowledge(store, "assistant") print(notes.index()) # the catalog of what the assistant knows print(notes.search("where does alice live")) Tests pytest ruff check . && ruff format --check . python examples/memory_benchmark.py # writes results/memory/ python examples/policy_benchmark.py # writes results/policies/ Previous Introduction Next Concepts

title: Leaderboard
text: Reference Leaderboard The memory benchmark as a leaderboard: each configuration ranked by accuracy, with the words it read and the log it kept. On this page How to read it The board is honest about where the library stands. Reading the whole history answers everything but costs the most words. Searching the episodic record answers about 96% of questions from about 20 words. The notes a rule-based extractor writes reach about 49%, and the oracle rows show the same pipeline reaching 100% when the extractor is perfect, so extraction quality is the limit, not the pipeline. How to read it Accuracy is the share of questions answered correctly, over the users and seeds shown. Reference rows are the two ends: no memory at all, and the full history in context. Oracle rows run an extractor that sees the truth. They are upper bounds for the notes pipeline, not results. Click a column to sort. Ranks stay with accuracy, so a sort does not change who is first. See Benchmarks for the protocol and its caveats, including that the paraphrases favour lexical search. Previous Benchmarks Next The log and the state

title: The log and the state
text: Internals The log and the state Status and tier are not stored on a memory. They are a fold over an append-only log, and every other feature is built on that. On this page Records and state Transactions Guards before, observers after Rollback is compensation Engines Records and state A Record puts, restores, retracts, or marks stale one memory, or moves it between tiers, inside a transaction, by an agent, at a time. State applies records in LSN order and keeps three indexes: by (kind, key), from each reference to the memories derived from it, and from each kind to the reads over it. Replaying the log rebuilds exactly the state that wrote it, and as_of(lsn) is a replay that stops early. Transactions All writes go through store.transaction(agent) . A transaction that raises writes nothing. Rewriting a live memory is a no-op, and a put of a known memory is a restore. On commit the store numbers the records, asks every guard, appends them to the engine in one call, applies them to the state, and then tells every observer. Guards before, observers after Guards reject a commit before it happens: scopes, provenance, a declared schema, a defender's checks. Observers react after it: caches, tier policies, schedulers. Neither may commit during a commit. An observer that wants to write calls store.defer(work) , and the store runs the work once the commit is done, in order. Rollback is compensation rollback_to(lsn) computes the state at that LSN and writes the records that move every memory back to its status and tier there, as ARIES does. Nothing is erased, so the log still shows what happened and what undid it. Engines Engine Where the log lives MemoryEngine A list, for tests. JsonlEngine One fsynced JSON line per transaction; a torn final line is dropped. SqliteEngine One SQLite transaction per commit, WAL journaling. Another backend subclasses Engine (two methods: append and records ; records_after and rewrite have defaults it may speed up) and registers in ENGINES . An engine can keep the log in an RDF store, so provenance questions become SPARQL: SELECT ?m WHERE { ?m <urn:memcommit:derivedFrom> <urn:memcommit:m:4e33527c048490ae> . } . Previous Leaderboard Next Provenance and invalidation

title: Notes
text: Using MemCommit Notes Notes are what was learned, short enough to read at the start of a session. Each records the episodes it came from. On this page Write and read notes Updates supersede, deletes retract The index Search and fetch Tools for a model Write and read notes from memcommit import Knowledge notes = Knowledge(store, "assistant") notes.add("user/alice/city", "Alice lives in Lyon.", tags=["profile"], derived_from=[turn.id]) notes.update("user/alice/city", "Alice moved to Paris.") notes.read("user/alice/city") # the live note notes.ls("user/alice") # live notes under a path notes.delete("user/alice/pet", "it was wrong") A path is a note's key. add raises if a live note is already there, and update raises if there is none. Updates supersede, deletes retract The log is immutable, so an update writes a new version and marks the old one stale. By default everything derived from the old version goes stale with it, since it was built on something that changed; pass cascade=False for a typo fix. Writing the same text again changes nothing. delete retracts: the note was wrong, and what was built on it falls too. The index print(notes.index(max_chars=4000)) # Memory index 4 notes. Use search_memory to find more, fetch_memory to read one. ## user/alice - city: alice lives in Lyon. [profile] - dog: alice's dog is Rex. [profile] The index is generated on demand, by directory, with each note's title (or first line) and tags. It is sized to a budget: the most important and most recent notes are kept first, and the tail says how many were left out. Inject it at the start of a session. Search and fetch notes.search("where does alice live", k=5, where="derived") # notes notes.search("allergic chicken", where="episodic") # what was said and done notes.search("cat", where="all") # both, by score notes.fetch("user/alice/city") # a note, in full notes.fetch(session.id) # a session id returns its transcript search spans both tiers, so an agent can recover detail a note dropped. fetch takes a note path or any memory id. Tools for a model notes.tools() returns five tool specs, each with a name , a description , and an input_schema : add_memory , update_memory , delete_memory , search_memory , and fetch_memory . notes.call(name, arguments, session=session) runs one and, with a session, records the call and its result in it. The shape is provider-neutral; an adapter maps it to a provider's format. notes.take_reads() returns the ids read since the last call, to pass as used to session.agent_says . Previous Sessions Next Dreaming

title: Playground
text: Try it Playground Write memories into an append-only log, say what each was derived from, retract a premise, and watch what was built on it go stale. Drag the log back in time, or roll it back. On this page Things to try What it keeps Warning This playground runs a JavaScript port of MemCommit's core , not the library. MemCommit is Python. The port covers content-addressed memories, restore on rewrite, retraction and invalidation with their cascades, rollback by compensating records, and as_of , and its tests replay scenarios recorded from the Python library and compare every id and log record. It does not port query references, guards, tiers beyond the first, or sessions, notes, and dreaming. For those, run memcommit demo ( Install ). Loading the playground… Things to try Load the demo and retract the first episode (it was wrong). It is withdrawn as a premise, and everything live built on it goes stale in the same transaction; the unrelated episode stays live. Mark stale is the softer version for something that is merely outdated. That is provenance . Write the same memory twice. A live memory with identical content is not written again. Write one that was retracted and it is restored: the id is a hash of the content, so redoing work that comes out the same names the same memory. Drag the slider back to see the state at an earlier log position, then press Roll back . The log is not rewritten: compensating records are appended, as in ARIES. Export the log to read it as JSON. What it keeps The operations you perform are saved in this browser (localStorage) and replayed when the page loads, so the log is the same after a reload. Clear the log to start again. Nothing is sent anywhere. Previous Concepts Next Declare a memory structure

title: Provenance and invalidation
text: Internals Provenance and invalidation Provenance is the lever the rest of MemCommit pulls. When a premise goes bad, everything built on it goes stale in one transaction. On this page derived_from Retraction Reads are provenance too In sessions and notes Memories are values derived_from derived_from holds memory ids and outside references ( doc:handbook@3 , file:sha256... ). invalidate(refs, reason) marks stale every live memory reachable through the reference index, in one transaction. A client that versions something outside the store (a document, a knowledge base, a model) records the version as a reference, and invalidating the version invalidates what was built on it. Retraction A commit that retracts a live memory marks stale everything built on it, directly or through a read whose result included it: work built on a premise that was withdrawn as wrong no longer holds. Memories written by the commit itself are left alone. Reads are provenance too An answer derives from the memories it read, but it also depends on the ones it looked for and did not find. "No notes about this topic" is built on an empty read, and the first note must undo it. So a reference can name a read: query_ref("note", topic="light") . An agent derives from it next to the memories the read returned. When a commit brings a memory live, the store finds the reads that memory now belongs to and marks everything built on them stale, in the same transaction. Only additions need this. A memory that drops out of a read was returned by it, so whatever used it already derives from it directly. Over-invalidation is cheap: work redone with the same result restores the same memory id. In sessions and notes A reply records the memories it read in derived_from . A note records the session and turns it came from. A summary records the steps it folds. So retracting a spoofed session stales the notes learned from it and the replies that used those notes, with no extra code. Memories are values A memory's id hashes its kind, key, body, source, scope, importance, and derived_from . A body cannot be changed without its id changing, so tampering shows up on load and in verify . Previous The log and the state Next The database underneath

title: Search and recall
text: Using MemCommit Search and recall Recall keeps an index in step with the store, so a stale memory is never recalled, and scores hits by relevance, recency, and importance. On this page Search Indexes Search across both tiers Search from memcommit import Recall recall = Recall(store, tiers=tiers) # tiers is optional hits = recall.search("speed of light", k=3, kinds=["fact"], scopes=["shared"], where={"unit": "km/s"}) for hit in hits: print(hit.memory.key, hit.score, hit.relevance, hit.recency, hit.importance) The score is a weighted sum of relevance (from the index), recency (decay per log record since the memory last changed), and importance. Filters: kinds , scopes , tiers (short and long by default; None searches all, including the archive), and where (body fields). With tiers given to Recall , hits are touched, which is how recall feeds the replacement policies; pass touch=False to leave counts alone. Indexes Index Needs Notes LexicalIndex nothing BM25 over the memory's kind, key, and body text. Lowercase terms, a small stopword list dropped, a light stemmer so live , lives , and lived agree. VectorIndex(embed) an embedding function Cosine similarity. embed maps a list of texts to a list of vectors. AnnIndex(embed, dimensions) an embedding function Approximate cosine search by random-hyperplane LSH with multi-probe, for many vectors. Every index is a Cache : CacheSync admits memories as they go live and evicts them when they stop holding, so a stale or retracted memory is never recalled. Note The lexical index matches words, not meaning. A paraphrase that shares no words with the query is not found; use VectorIndex for that. The benchmark in Benchmarks is built so its paraphrases share words with the questions, which favours lexical search. Search across both tiers Knowledge.search(query, k, where) searches notes ( derived ), what was said and done ( episodic ), or both ( all ), and returns plain dictionaries. See Notes . Previous Dreaming Next Working memory

title: Roadmap
text: Project Roadmap Every feature in the plan is built and tested. Next are the gaps the benchmarks found. On this page Built Next Built The log-structured store, the declared structure, episodic sessions, derived notes with an index and agent tools, offline consolidation, the cache and its policies, compaction of memories and of the log, recall, the blackboard, audit, the server, a demo, and two benchmarks. Next A model-backed extractor. The built-in extractor finds about half the facts in the benchmark, and a perfect one reaches 1.000. A language model behind the Extractor signature is the largest open gain. Deduplication across paths. Near-duplicates are merged only within a directory. Meaning, not words. The lexical index cannot match a paraphrase that shares no words with the query. VectorIndex can; the benchmark does not yet test it. Recorded conversations. Both benchmarks are synthetic. The same harness should run on recorded conversations, with a model as reader. A provider adapter from Knowledge.tools() to a provider's tool format. New work starts as an experiment: a recorded workload or a policy to compare, measured and written to results/ . Previous Decisions

title: Sessions
text: Using MemCommit Sessions A session is a trace with conversational helpers. Every turn, tool call, and result is its own memory, committed as it happens. On this page Record a session Tool calls Replies derive from what they read Find sessions What is stored Record a session from memcommit import Session with Session.start(store, "assistant", user="alice") as session: session.user_says("I live in Lyon.") lookup = session.wrap(search_web, "search_web") # calls recorded with their results lookup(query="weather in Lyon") session.agent_says("Noted.") Leaving the block ends the session ok , or error if it raised. Each step commits on its own, so a crash keeps what was said. Session.open(store, root_id) reads one back, session.transcript() lists its turns, calls, and results in order, and session.text() renders them as text. Tool calls session.call(tool, arguments, run) runs run(**arguments) , recording an action before and an observation after, or an error if it raised (and re-raising). session.wrap(function, name) returns the function with every call recorded, as a plugin would. Replies derive from what they read session.agent_says("Alice lives in Lyon.", used=notes.take_reads()) used are the memories the reply was built on. If one is later retracted, the reply goes stale. Find sessions from memcommit import Episodes episodes = Episodes(store) episodes.sessions(user="alice", ended=True) # oldest first episodes.new_since(lsn) # sessions that ended after a point in the log new_since is what an offline pass reads. See Dreaming . What is stored A session is a trace root with the task session and the user in its inputs. User and agent turns are message steps with a role ; calls are action steps; results are observation steps. Nothing is distilled away, so detail a summary dropped can still be fetched. Previous Declare a memory structure Next Notes

title: The database underneath
text: Internals The database underneath MemCommit is a log-structured store, and it borrows a database's answers to a database's problems. On this page Two levels of compaction Retention Snapshots Seals One writer, many readers Two levels of compaction Memory compaction decides what agents see: finished traces fold into summaries, cold mid-term segments consolidate, summaries of the same task merge. It never deletes; it moves memories to the archive. Log compaction decides what the disk holds. A memory's history can be long (put, stale, restore, stale, move), but replaying its state needs three records: the put, the last status change, and the last move. storage.compact keeps exactly those, as the original records, up to a horizon, and keeps every record after the horizon verbatim, so the folded log replays to the same state. That is the LSM move: rewrite the sorted history into something smaller that answers the same reads. The price is history inside the horizon. from memcommit.storage import ArchivedOlderThan, compact report = compact(store, retention=ArchivedOlderThan(seconds=30 * 86400)) print(report.before, "->", report.after, "records; purged", len(report.purged)) Retention Purging is the one place a memory leaves the log. It happens only during log compaction, only for memories a retention policy names ( ArchivedOlderThan , KindsAfter , or any RetentionPolicy ), and only for memories with no record after the horizon. A compaction manifest lists them, so a later reference to a purged memory is known to be deliberate, not forged. Snapshots store.save_snapshot("state.json") store = memcommit.open("memory.db", snapshot="state.json") # replays only the records after it A snapshot is the state as JSON. Opening from one reads only the records after it. Seals seal(store) writes a hash chain over the log up to an LSN; AutoSeal(store, every=1000) seals every N records; check_seal rechecks the newest and verify rechecks all of them after the last compaction. Compaction invalidates every earlier seal by design, so the manifest stores the old log's chain and a new seal covers the new log. One writer, many readers LSNs must come from one place. python -m memcommit serve memory.db runs a MemoryServer that owns the log and runs every commit, so guards hold across processes. RemoteStore(url) is a MemoryStore on it, and store.refresh() pulls commits other processes made. A refused commit raises Rejected in the client. AsyncMemoryStore commits in a worker thread, one at a time, for an event loop. Previous Provenance and invalidation Next Decisions

title: Declare a memory structure
text: Using MemCommit Declare a memory structure MemCommit's core knows no domain. A project declares its own kinds once, as a schema, and a commit guard enforces it for every writer. On this page A schema of kinds What a kind says The body schema Provenance is declared with structure Evolving a schema Showing the structure A schema of kinds from memcommit import Kind, Schema schema = Schema( Kind("question", body={"type": "object", "required": ["text"]}), Kind( "answer", description="what an agent concluded", body={ "type": "object", "required": ["text", "confidence"], "properties": {"confidence": {"type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 1}}, }, requires=("question",), scopes=("shared", "agent"), tier="long", importance=0.5, ), strict=True, name="support", ) schema.attach(store) attach adds the guard and records the schema in the log. From then on a commit that puts a memory out of line with its kind is rejected before it is written, with every problem named. What a kind says Field Meaning body A JSON schema for the body. scopes Where it may be written: shared , agent (the writer's own scope or one under it), or any scope name. None allows any. requires Kinds it must be derived from. A memory of this kind must list at least one memory of each in derived_from . A premise written in the same commit counts. tier , importance Defaults that schema.put(store, agent, kind, key, body) fills in. strict=True rejects kinds the schema does not declare. The kinds MemCommit writes itself (traces and their steps, summaries, receipts, seals, the compaction manifest, notes, dream records, the schema) are always allowed. The body schema A small JSON-schema subset, with no dependency: type ( object , array , string , number , integer , boolean , null , or a list), properties , required , additionalProperties ( false to forbid extras), items , enum , minimum , maximum , minLength , maxLength , minItems , maxItems . A schema written in it is also valid JSON Schema. Provenance is declared with structure requires is how a structure also says what a memory must be built on. An answer that names no question is rejected, so a memory cannot be written with its lineage missing, and invalidating a question reaches its answers. Evolving a schema The schema is itself a memory. Recording a changed schema writes a new schema memory and marks the previous one stale, so as_of(lsn) shows which structure held when. Schema.load(store, name) reads the live one back, and schema.version is a short hash of its content. Old data is not revalidated when the schema changes. schema.audit(store) returns the live memories that no longer conform, by id. Showing the structure schema.describe() returns the structure as Markdown, one section per kind, which is what an agent can read to know what it may write. Note Kinds other systems write to the same store are not checked unless strict is on. The Agentic Ontologist's STRUCTURE is declared this way: it checks question , answer , and agent-run steps, and leaves KROMA's and Aegis's kinds alone. Previous Playground Next Sessions

title: Working memory
text: Using MemCommit Working memory The store holds every memory; short-term memory holds the few an agent works with now. It is a cache, and its policies are pluggable. On this page Configure the tiers What maintenance does Hits and misses Policies Mid-term segments Compaction of memories Configure the tiers from memcommit import ( AccessCount, AnyOf, Compactor, ImportanceAtLeast, KeepFailed, KindIn, Scored, TieredMemory, ) tiers = TieredMemory( store, capacity=64, # per partition; a partition is a scope by default eviction=Scored(recency=1.0, importance=1.0, frequency=0.5), promotion=AnyOf(AccessCount(3), ImportanceAtLeast(0.8), KindIn(["decision"])), compactor=Compactor(store, policy=KeepFailed(records=5000), summarizer=my_summary), mid_capacity=256, heat_threshold=10.0, # a mid-term tier of segments long_capacity=10_000, ) tiers.touch([m.id for m in context]) # count a use; archived memories are paged back in tiers.working(scopes=["shared", "planner"]) # what is in working memory tiers.maintain() # runs on its own when a partition goes over capacity What maintenance does When a commit leaves a partition over capacity, maintain() runs after the commit, through store.defer : Compact finished traces into long-term summaries. Promote what the promotion policy selects to long-term. Evict from each short-term partition over capacity, memories that no longer hold first, then the eviction policy's victims, to the archive (or to mid-term). Trim long-term to its capacity, if it has one. Hits and misses touch is a cache access: a hit when the memory is in short-term memory, a warm hit when it is in mid- or long-term, and a miss when it is archived or no longer holds. A missed live memory is paged back in, and eviction makes room. tiers.stats counts them. Policies Eviction Idea FIFO , LRU , LFU The classics. TwoQueue , ARC Scan-resistant and adaptive (ghost lists). Forgetting An Ebbinghaus curve: what is used often or marked important fades slowest. Scored A weighted recency, importance, and frequency score. TTL A time to live by kind. Learned An online logistic model. Promotion policies are AccessCount , ImportanceAtLeast , KindIn , AnyOf , AllOf , and Never . A policy is any object with victims(candidates, n, now) or select(candidates, now) ; a candidate carries the memory, its tier and status, and its use counts on a logical clock. Stateful policies are told about each use, eviction, and page-in. Mid-term segments With mid_capacity , evicted memories wait in the mid tier grouped into segments (by trace). A segment past heat_threshold is promoted whole; while mid-term is over capacity, the coldest segment is consolidated into one summary and archived. Compaction of memories Compactor turns a finished trace into a long-term summary derived from the root and every step, and moves the steps to the archive, in one transaction. Policies choose which traces: FinishedTraces , OlderThan , KeepFailed , UnderPressure . Compactor.merge folds summaries of the same task into one. A summarizer is any function from a Trace to JSON; outline needs no model. Previous Search and recall Next Agents and scopes
